theme: Kingdom parables; John beheaded; the feeding
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 13:24-14:36. Jesus tells more parables of the kingdom, is rejected in Nazareth, and hears of John’s death. Then he feeds five thousand and walks on the sea. Notice Peter in the boat.
settingTheScene: The parables of Matthew 13 explain what the kingdom is like now that the King is here. It is not what many expected, an immediate military takeover. It begins small, grows slowly, and exists alongside evil until the end. Then the narrative moves quickly: Jesus is rejected at home, John the Baptist is killed, and the crowds are fed. In each scene, the identity of Jesus is the question.
observation: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field” (13:31).
“The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour” (13:33).
“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (13:44).
“And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief” (13:58).
“They took up his body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus” (14:12).
“Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid” (14:27).
interpretation:
The parables of the weeds, mustard seed, and leaven teach that the kingdom starts small and spreads quietly, and that good and evil grow together until the harvest. The wheat and the weeds will be separated at the end, and not before. This protects us from two errors: trying to purify the church by force, and thinking that evil has won.

The treasure and the pearl show the worth of the kingdom. A man finds treasure and sells everything for joy. This is not grudging sacrifice but delighted exchange. Following Jesus costs everything, and it is worth it.

Then comes rejection. In his hometown, the people take offense at him: “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” Familiarity breeds contempt. Matthew says he did not do many works there because of unbelief.

When Jesus hears about John’s death, he withdraws to a quiet place, but the crowds follow. He has compassion and heals them. In the evening, the disciples want to send the people away. Jesus says, “You give them something to eat.” With five loaves and two fish, he feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, with twelve baskets left over. It echoes the manna in the wilderness and anticipates the Lord’s Supper.

Then Jesus sends the disciples ahead in the boat and goes up to pray. In the storm he comes walking on the sea, which only God does (Job 9:8). Peter steps out, walks, sees the wind, and begins to sink. “Lord, save me.” Jesus catches him. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”
connection: Daniel 2:34-35 and 44-45 compare the kingdom to a stone that becomes a mountain. Ezekiel 17:22-24 uses the image of a tree where birds nest. Philippians 3:7-8 shows Paul counting all things as loss for Christ. Exodus 16 describes manna in the wilderness. Job 9:8 says God alone treads on the waves of the sea. Psalm 77:19 says God’s way was through the sea. John 6:35: “I am the bread of life.” Hebrews 12:2 says to look to Jesus.
application:
Think of the kingdom like treasure. Is there something you are holding too tightly that you would be glad to exchange for it?

When Jesus says, “You give them something to eat,” ask what small thing you can offer. He can multiply it.

When you start to sink, say Peter’s prayer: “Lord, save me.”
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus what you are holding too tightly.
Ask him to teach you to treasure the kingdom above all.
